extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of 19th-century nautical exploration and natural-history travel writing (navigators, hydrographers, naturalists, and general readers of travel narratives)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and observational practices for producing a nautical exploration / natural-history travel narrative: includes standards for navigation and charting, surveying passages, recording tides/flora/fauna, and documenting encounters with indigenous peoples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using magnetic north alone for land boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not lay down boundary lines by magnetic north without accounting for variation; using magnetic north instead of true north produces shifting boundaries over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The variation at Sydney has progressively increased since the colony's formation, causing differences as large as one square mile in ten for a boundary. Local attraction and inconsistent needles compound the problem. Surveyors must account for magnetic variation (or use true bearings) to prevent endless disputes and litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set land-pricing policy to encourage settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: High minimum prices for land sales (e.g., one pound per acre) discourage small capitalists and retard emigration and development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to raise the largest sum by selling the smallest number of allotments is unwise; it may be more advantageous to subsidize or give away some land to encourage occupancy and development. The author calculates that selling the whole continent at one pound/acre would realize a very large sum, but it would hinder settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rate chronometers and repeat magnetic observations before proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow time at anchorage to rate chronometers and perform magnetic observations to ensure accurate navigation and positioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Beagle remained five days at Magnetical Island to rate chronometers and examine Halifax Bay. Before leaving Cape Upstart they repeated meridian distances and magnetic observations; such procedures are essential preparatory work for reliable surveying and chart correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify and correct existing charts with direct bearings and positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare charted positions to observed bearings and ranges; correct charts where features are misplaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cape Otway projected three or four miles too much on the charts; Snapper Island and the coast were placed too far east. Use visible summits and measured bearings (e.g., 'summit of Snapper Island bore South 7 degrees East six miles') to fix positions and amend charts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey passages with boats and soundings to determine navigability by draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore straits and inlets with whaleboats or small craft, take soundings at low water, and record least depths to determine if larger vessels can pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author led boats through Endeavour Strait and recorded least water (e.g., 3 1/2 fathoms at low tide), concluding it was navigable for vessels drawing 18 feet. Note distances from islands and recommended tracks (e.g., 'passing about a mile and a half to the northward of the Wallis Islands').

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe and record tidal phenomena and timings
rubrics_metrics.description: Document tidal patterns, timing of high/low water, flood/ebb duration, and current directions/velocities for safe navigation and accurate descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record local anomalies (e.g., tides ebbing and flowing twelve hours) and precise timings: 'At the entrance of Van Diemen's Inlet it is high-water on the full and change of the moon at a quarter to seven; in the upper part the tides are three hours and a quarter later; the length of both flood and ebb is twelve hours.' Note velocity (e.g., flood-stream two knots) and variation between anchorages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record natural-history observations and collect specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe and, when appropriate, collect specimens of birds, mammals, plants, and other natural objects with careful notes on appearance, behaviour, and locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. Bynoe procured pigeons (Ptilinopus superbus) with detailed colour notes; noting egg counts (painted quail lays four eggs vs quails 14–15); record habitat (e.g., mangroves, sand dunes), abundance of species (turtles, wallaby), and locations (lat/long). Specimen collection and description enrich the travel narrative and scientific record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document interactions with indigenous peoples: language, dress, tools, and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: When encountering natives, record observable cultural details — language fragments, bodily adornment, weapons, boats, dances, and reactions to the ship — with sensitivity and specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Torres Strait natives recognized Murray Island canoe drawings and repeated the word 'toolic' meaning iron; ear lobes perforated with bone; spears pointed with bone and fishing shafts with coil of line. Describe ceremonies (corrobory): painted bodies, dance movements, and unique features (boomerang set alight, producing a bright line of fire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain and repair shared records and visitor logs at waypoints
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep and preserve post-office books and visitor registers on remote islands; repair or replace them if damaged so subsequent visitors can leave records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Booby Island the Post Office book had been destroyed; the party repaired the box and left a new book with pens and ink. Maintaining such records aids navigation history and community knowledge among visiting ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify prior reports and hypotheses by direct observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely solely on previous reports; test claims (e.g., of estuaries or large bays) by landing and examining the locality to confirm or refute earlier accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author examined Halifax Bay and found no large estuary reported by Captain King, concluding King had been deceived by mirage. Use on-site investigation (landing parties, surveying) to resolve conflicting reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and locate sources of fresh water (native wells, springs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek and record freshwater sources such as native wells and springs when exploring low-lying coasts and inlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fresh water on these coasts may be scarce; the only fresh water found in one inlet was at a native well half a mile south-east from the eastern entrance point. Verify existing wells (e.g., 'Investigator's well') and note their positions for resupply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate signalling and anchoring practices when approaching inhabited islands at night
rubrics_metrics.description: When arriving at night near islands with natives, use signals (e.g., rockets) and careful anchoring to avoid alarm and to establish peaceful contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On arriving at Restoration Island at night the discharge of a signal rocket quieted the initial yell of startled natives and restored silence. Anchor selection should consider confined anchorages and the presence of multiple ships.
